4) Tokenization & max_tokens: we should estimate token usage from your prompts + context. Dev will provide guidance on tokenization and stop sequences.
5) Streaming semantics: you wanted partial results in the UI \u0014 we'll outline how streaming tokens and stop sequences interact.

Attachments: redwood-sdk-quickstart.pdf, redwood-auth-flow.png (high level auth diagrams).

Subject: Re: Acme \u0014 request/response schema + tokenization/streaming notes

Hi Sam \u0014 thanks for the schema and notes. A few concrete answers and recommendations below (focused on engineering/implementation):

1) Chat vs Completions (short):
- Chat API (recommended): first-class support for role-based messages, function/tool-calling for strongly-typed outputs, and better fit for multi-turn contexts.
- Completions: OK for single-prompt outputs, but you lose the tooling/function schema orchestration available in the chat API.

2) Structured output + function/tool-calling:
- Pattern: declare a function with a JSON schema that matches your ticket object. The model returns a function call with args that you can validate and process server-side. This avoids brittle free-form parsing.
- Example function signature (pseudocode):
  function create_ticket({"intent": "string", "issue_type": "string", "priority": "string", "summary": "string", "actions": [{"type":"string","params":"object"}]})

3) Tokenization and max_tokens calculation:
- Our tokenization uses the same BPE tokenizer family as the model. Rough heuristic: 1.3 tokens per English word (varies).
- Practical calc: 
  a) Run your prompt + top-K context through our tokenizer (we can run this for your sample prompts).
  b) Set max_tokens = model_context_limit - tokenized_context_length - margin.
- Example: for a 4k-context model, if your context + system messages tokenizes to 2800 tokens, reserve ~512-1024 tokens for model output depending on how long you expect the ticket JSON to be.

4) Stop sequences & streaming semantics:
- Streaming: we stream token deltas as they are generated; function-calls are signaled via a structured call event. Partial tokens may arrive in the UI \u0014 do not apply stop-sequence trimming client-side until you receive the final event unless you need early truncation.
- Stop sequences: they are applied server-side to prevent generation past a sentinel; if used with streaming, the final event will indicate completion/reason (stop sequence or max_tokens). If you rely on stop sequences for clean JSON termination, prefer function-calling which returns a complete args payload rather than relying on stop tokens to terminate free-form JSON.

5) Embeddings / reranker notes:
- Batch embeddings for throughput; use async bulk endpoints for indexing. For reranking, pass the top-N candidates with lightweight features (score + metadata) into a reranker model or run a small cross-encoder. We recommend caching embeddings for immutable KB docs and re-computing for new tickets only.

6) Security / deployment modes:
- SOC2 artifacts: we can share SOC2 reports and security whitepapers.
- KMS/HSM: Private deployments have customer-managed KMS. Dedicated (Redwood-managed infra) supports envelope encryption with customer KMS integrations for key wrapping; we can walk your security team through options.

7) Action items for engineering work: 
- Send a couple of real prompt+context examples (we'll run tokenizer counts and return estimates).
- We'll prepare a starter function-schema JSON and a sample chat request/response with streaming events.

Quick reference links: https://docs.redwood.ai/api/chat, https://docs.redwood.ai/guides/streaming, https://docs.redwood.ai/security/soc2

If you want, we can run a short script against your example prompts to show token counts \u0014 I can take that on once you send samples.

Thanks \u0014 Dev
